Founded in 2000, Diamond Hill Capital (Trades, Portfolio) Management, Inc. is a registered investment adviser headquartered in Columbus, Ohio. Diamond Hill manages a diverse range of equity strategies, including traditional and alternative options, available through various investment vehicles such as separately managed accounts, mutual funds, and private investment funds. Diamond Hill's investment approach is primarily bottom-up, focusing on fundamental analysis of a company's profitability, market position, and management quality, among other factors. The firm also considers industry dynamics and regulatory environments in its top-down analysis, eschewing macroeconomic factors. title: Broadcom shares slump as OpenAI’s $18B custom chip deal hits financing snag
content:
Investing.com -- Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) shares fell 4% Thursday afternoon following a report that its AI chip deal with OpenAI has encountered an $18 billion financing obstacle.

The companies are negotiating an agreement for Broadcom to finance the first phase of chip production, which would consume 1.3 GW of data center capacity and cost around $18 billion, according to The Information, citing an internal memo and two people involved in the talks.

The negotiations have hit a potential snag, as Broadcom has said it would finance the first phase only if Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) agrees to buy roughly 40% of the chips, an OpenAI executive told colleagues in a memo last month. Under the proposed arrangement, Microsoft would install the chips in its data centers and then rent them back to OpenAI.

A purchase commitment from Microsoft would give Broadcom confidence it would get its money back, according to a person involved in the talks. However, Microsoft could choose not to buy OpenAI’s chips, which would change the financing terms for the project, the memo said.

Securing the financing is important for OpenAI because the ChatGPT maker has projected its operations will burn more than $200 billion through 2029. Using its own chips is central to OpenAI’s ambition to lower its server costs and improve its gross profit margins.

title: OpenAI Tesla Merger Idea Emerges In Trial
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) CEO Elon Musk once pushed to bring OpenAI into Tesla and even offered OpenAI CEO Sam Altman a seat on Tesla's board, according to testimony from former OpenAI board member Shivon Zilis.

The comments came during an ongoing court battle tied to Musk's lawsuit against OpenAI, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT).

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA. Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Zilis testified that between 2017 and 2018, OpenAI's leadership debated different corporate structures extensively, including whether the AI company should evolve into a for-profit business. At one point, Musk reportedly proposed folding OpenAI into Tesla as part of that process.

The testimony adds another layer to the increasingly public split between Musk and OpenAI. Musk co-founded the company in 2015 and reportedly contributed about $38 million in early funding before leaving the board in 2018 after disagreements over control. He is now suing OpenAI and its leadership for more than $130B, arguing the organization abandoned its nonprofit mission. OpenAI has pushed back, saying Musk understood the company's commercial ambitions from early on.

The trial also highlights how closely tied the early AI ecosystem was to major tech and automotive players before the current AI boom reshaped the industry. Since leaving OpenAI, Musk launched xAI, which has since merged with SpaceX, creating a direct competitor in the AI race.

title: DeepL To Cut 25% Of Workforce As AI Reshapes Translation Market
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

DeepL is entering a leaner chapter as artificial intelligence starts to reshape the translation software market from the inside. The German startup announced plans to cut approximately 25% of its workforce, equal to about 250 employees, subject to legal processes. Chief Executive Officer Jarek Kutylowski attributed the move to what he described as a massive structural shift from artificial intelligence. Kutylowski said adapting the company to work more effectively with AI means fewer layers, faster decisions and far less time spent on the back and forth that can slow large teams down. For investors watching private AI software companies, the message could be important: AI is not only creating new demand, it is also possibly forcing companies to rethink how much structure they need to compete.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 2 Warning Sign with META. Is META fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The decision comes as technology companies are cutting jobs while redirecting resources toward AI products and automation. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) announced plans last month to cut 10% of its workers, while Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is offering buyouts to about 7% of its US workforce. DeepL's move fits into that broader pattern, where AI tools are replacing work traditionally done by programmers and companies are trying to build more efficient operating models around their own AI products. That could make the restructuring especially relevant for investors, because the next phase of the AI cycle may not only be about revenue growth, but also about how companies manage costs, speed and organizational complexity.

Founded in 2017 and based in Cologne, DeepL built its business as a rival to Google Translate, offering AI-powered translation tools that help developers build applications in multiple languages. More recently, the company has had to compete with translation services offered by ChatGPT and other AI tools, creating a more crowded market for language software. DeepL raised $300 million at a $2 billion valuation in 2024 and has weighed a US initial public offering. The cuts could therefore be read as a possible signal that DeepL is preparing for a market where faster execution, sharper focus and differentiation may matter more as AI changes both the product landscape and the cost base behind it.

title: Microsoft Reconsiders Energy Goal Amid AI Boom
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is reportedly reconsidering one of its biggest climate goals as the AI driven data center boom pushes energy demand to new levels.

According to reports, the company is discussing whether to delay or potentially abandon its 2030 target of matching 100% of its hourly electricity usage with renewable energy purchases. The conversations are still ongoing and no final decision has been made, but the debate itself highlights how quickly AI infrastructure demands are reshaping energy priorities across Big Tech.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 1 Warning Sign with MSFT. Is MSFT fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The challenge comes down to scale. Microsoft has been adding nearly 1 gigawatt of data center capacity every 3 months as it races to support AI and cloud growth. That rapid expansion is increasing both electricity usage and emissions, despite major renewable energy investments. Since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, Microsoft's emissions have reportedly risen 23%, with the company itself pointing to AI and cloud expansion as major contributors.

At the same time, the industry is increasingly leaning toward natural gas to meet near term power needs. Companies like Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META) and Google (GOOG) are also facing growing pressure as AI workloads surge. Microsoft says it remains committed to its long term sustainability ambitions, but also acknowledged that adjustments may be needed as markets and technology evolve.
